segments.text: "Name" — native, as you'd expect from Tamil's closest sister.
(Skim if you read Malayalam.) പ (pa) + േ (the ē-sign) becomes പേ (pē); ര് (bare r, chandrakkala). Read പേ, ര് becomes pēru.

പേര് (pēru, "name") is native Dravidian, from Proto-Dravidian pēr — the same word as Tamil peyar and Telugu pēru, a cousin of Kannada hesaru (p becomes h). Being Tamil's closest sister, Malayalam keeps the native word, not Sanskrit nāma (Hindi nām, English name).

segments.text: Before the new one: പ (pa) — what does it do?
One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with ē. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
Look at പേര് (pēr) again. The പ you read on the page before carries an a of its own — pa. The hook standing in front of it, േ, takes that a away and puts a long ē in its place: pa becomes pē.

Malayalam prints this sign to the LEFT of its consonant even though the vowel is pronounced AFTER it. Your eye reads it first; your mouth says it second.

lessons.title: ആണ് (āṇŭ) — "is," where Malayalam breaks with its sisters
lessons.gloss: is (the copula)

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: A small surprise: Malayalam has a real word for "is," where its Dravidian sisters have none.
(Skim if you read Malayalam.) ആ (independent long ā) + ണ് (bare retroflex ṇ) becomes āṇŭ.
ആണ് (āṇŭ, "is") is Malayalam's copula — a real "to be" word, grown from the verb ആക (āka, "to be, to become").

Here's the point: Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu all use the zero copula — no word for "is." Yet Malayalam, though it is Tamil's closest sister, grammaticalised a "to be" verb. So where Tamil says only eṉ peyar Arun, Malayalam adds āṇŭ: enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the verb comes last

segments.text: Like Hindi's hai (and unlike Tamil), āṇŭ closes the sentence — Malayalam is subject–object–verb: "my name Arun is." (Malayalis sometimes drop āṇŭ in fast speech, but the full form keeps it.)

segments.text: Assemble the three atoms — including the copula āṇŭ that Tamil lacks.
enṟe (my) + pēru (name) + your name + āṇŭ (is).

lessons.title: നിന്റെ പേര് എന്താണ്? (ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?) — "what's your name?"
lessons.gloss: what's your name?

segments.text: Assemble the question — your + name + what-is. And notice the copula hiding in the last word.
നിന്റെ (ninṟe, "your") = the possessive of nī ("you").
എന്താണ് (entāṇŭ) = entŭ (what) + āṇŭ (is), fused into one.
നിന്റെ പേര് എന്താണ്? (ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?) = literally "your name what is?"
Unlike the Tamil question (which had no verb), Malayalam carries its copula āṇŭ right inside the question-word entāṇŭ.

blocks.title: The exchange — the words you can use

segments.text: സന്തോഷം (santōṣam) literally means "joy." At the end of a short introduction, it can stand by itself for "pleased to meet you." A fuller phrase exists, but it needs words and grammar you have not learned yet; the one-word version is complete and useful now.

blocks.title: Script: two new shapes to notice

segments.text: Keep സന്തോഷം (santōṣam) visible. Most of its shapes have already appeared in this chapter. Point to just two new ones:
ഷ carries the ṣa sound near the end.
ോ is the long ō vowel sign attached to the consonant before it.
Look, point, and say the whole word once. The next two-minute lesson will let your hand copy it with the model still present.

സന്തോഷം (santōṣam, "joy") is Sanskrit — the same loan Kannada and Telugu use. So even Malayalam, the great keeper of native words (recall nandi for "thanks" in Chapter 1), reaches for Sanskrit here. The loanwords spread selectively, word by word — which is exactly what these cognate notes trace: native for "name" and "thanks," Sanskrit for "pleased."

segments.text: Before the new one: ൾ (ḷ) — what does it do?
One character this time. One only. It has not been on a page yet: it arrives with the word on the next one.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with u. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
The dialogue on the next page introduces two people by name, and one of the names carries this sign.
അരുൺ aruṇ — a common man's name in Kerala.
The sign hangs under its consonant and replaces that consonant's built-in a with u: ര ra becomes രു ru.
Put your pen on ◌ു and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ു (u) — what does it do?
One character this time. One only. It has not been on a page yet: it arrives with the word on the next one.
ൺ — ṇ.
It is a chillu — a consonant with its vowel stripped away and given a shape of its own, so that it can end a word without a dangling mark.
The same name ends with one, and it is the second chillu you have met.
അരുൺ aruṇ — the name you are about to read.
നിങ്ങൾ niṅṅaḷ — you, respectful, ending in ൾ.
ൺ is ണ — the ṇa you read two pages ago — with its a handed back and an end-of-word shape of its own. Hold ണ and ൺ side by side.

segments.text: Point to സന്തോഷം and say santōṣam once. Keep the model on the page. Find ഷ near the end, then find the long ō sign ോ on the consonant before it. Those are the two shapes you will work with.
Look at ഷ and ോ without writing. Say ṣa and ō. The first action is observe and trace: your finger follows a visible model, so memory is not yet doing the work.

Trace ഷ once and ോ once with your finger while both models remain visible. Stop after those two shapes. The next action is a guided copy: the whole word stays in view while your hand makes its own copy.
Follow സന്തോഷം (santōṣam) from left to right with your finger. Then copy the whole word once directly below the visible model. Look back as often as you need.
This is shape familiarity, not a stroke-order test. Write large and slowly. Do not hide the model, do not spell from memory, and do not add a second word.
Compare your copy with സന്തോഷം while both remain visible. Check only the two shapes you noticed: ഷ and ോ. Repair one shape if you want, then stop and say santōṣam once more.

utterances: എന്റെ പേര് മീരാ ആണ്. (enṟe pēru Mira āṇŭ) means My name is Mira.
നിന്റെ പേര് എന്താണ്? (ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?) (ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ) means What's your name?
എന്റെ പേര് അരുൺ ആണ്. (enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ) means My name is Arun.
സന്തോഷം. (santōṣam) means Pleased to meet you.

segments.text: Every atom traced:
pēru from Dravidian pēr (not name; twin of Tamil peyar).
enṟe — the native Dravidian possessive "my".
āṇŭ from the verb āka ("to be") — Malayalam's copula.
entŭ from Dravidian question-stem yā-/e-.
santōṣam from Sanskrit (borrowed even in native-loving Malayalam).
The Malayalam standout: unlike its Dravidian sisters' zero copula, Malayalam has a word for "is" (āṇŭ) — a real grammatical difference between the closest of sisters.
